name: Casanova di Neri Brunello di Montalcino Tenuta Nuova 2011
text:
## Casanova di Neri Brunello di Montalcino Tenuta Nuova 2011

**The story.** Casanova di Neri was founded in 1971 by Giovanni Neri in the north-east of [Montalcino](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Casanova+di+Neri,+Podere+Fiesole,+Montalcino,+Italy&t=k), in the Canalicchio area. The property covers 500 hectares, of which 63 are vines; the rest is woodland, olive groves and farmland. His son Giacomo and grandsons Giovanni and Gianlorenzo now run it, and Fine+Rare credits the estate with pioneering the idea of single-vineyard [Brunello di Montalcino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunello_di_Montalcino) ([Fine+Rare](https://frw.co.uk/producer/612ec28006000000000005d6/casanova-di-neri)). The vines are spread across seven vineyards at 300 to 450 metres. The family's obsession is ripe, sweet tannins: Sangiovese's reputation, they say, suffers from poorly handled, harsh tannins, so all the fruit is destemmed and sorted by hand and then by an optical sorter, so only perfectly ripe berries reach the tank.

**The wine: Tenuta Nuova.** "Tenuta Nuova" means "new estate". It comes from a south-facing vineyard of very stony, rocky ground that, according to Fine+Rare, gives distinctive rosemary and eucalyptus notes and real persistence. It is 100% [Sangiovese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangiovese), as Brunello must be. Its big brother, Cerretalto, grows on graphite-rich soil on a very steep slope ([Fine+Rare](https://frw.co.uk/producer/612ec28006000000000005d6/casanova-di-neri)).

**Brunello in brief.** "Brunello", from *bruno*, brown, was the local name for what was thought to be a separate grape; in 1879 Siena's ampelographic commission found it was Sangiovese. In the mid-19th century Clemente Santi isolated Sangiovese plantings to make a pure, long-lived wine, and his grandson Ferruccio Biondi-Santi, who had fought under [Garibaldi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Garibaldi), carried it on. In 1980 Brunello was one of the first four Italian wines to win [DOCG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denominazione_di_origine_controllata) status ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunello_di_Montalcino)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [Tuscany vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/tuscany) calls 2011 "an exceptionally hot vintage with a very irregular weather pattern": a cold, snowy winter, a hot April, a cool May, then record-breaking heat in mid-August that made the grapes seem prematurely ready, with some producers picking at the end of August to save the fruit. Many wines are rich but still have enough freshness, though she doubts it will last through prolonged ageing. Casanova di Neri's obsession with ripe, sweet tannins and strict sorting suited such a year.

**What the critics say for 2011.**
- **Falstaff: 95** (Othmar Kiem and Simon Staffler, 2018, [Falstaff](https://www.falstaff.com/en/wines/casanova-di-neri-2011-brunello-di-montalcino-docg-tenuta-nuova)). Shiny, intense ruby; a dense, appealing nose of nougat, then lots of raspberry and cherry, "open and accessible"; dense texture, finely meshed tannins, blackberry notes and grip. Falstaff had rated it 96 in an earlier tasting in March 2016.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 92.9** (from your CellarTracker list).
- (I couldn't read Wine Advocate, Wine Spectator or Suckling scores for the 2011, so I've left them out.)

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is fifteen years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2017 to 2030, and Jancis Robinson doubts the freshness of hot 2011s will last through prolonged ageing. So drink it over the next few years, while the cherry and raspberry fruit is still generous. Decant an hour or two ahead.

**Serving.** Decant Brunello an hour or two ahead. Vinous advised that Casanova di Neri's 2012s benefit greatly from "four to five hours in the glass" ([Bordeaux Index](https://bordeauxindex.com/fine-wine/italy/tuscany/castn-2012)). Serve at about 17°C.

**Food.** Brunello loves Tuscan food: [bistecca alla fiorentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bistecca_alla_fiorentina), wild boar stew ([cinghiale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_boar)), [pici](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pici) with ragù, roast lamb, porcini, or aged [Pecorino Toscano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pecorino_toscano).

**Value and where to buy.** Casanova di Neri is very well stocked here: ZYN has the Tenuta Nuova 2021 at $219, the Brunello 2020 and 2021 from $96, Cerretalto 2019 at $790, Rosso di Montalcino Giovanni at $129, IrRosso at $50.50 and Pietradonice Cabernet at $179; BC Liquor has the Tenuta Nuova at $230.97, the Brunello 2013 at $115.99 and Cerretalto at $780.

**From the history books**
- **A medieval wine.** One of the first records of a "Brunello" is a red wine from Montalcino in the early 14th century; in 1831 the Marchese Cosimo Ridolfi praised Montalcino's reds above all others in Tuscany ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunello_di_Montalcino)).
- **A prize in 1865.** An agricultural fair in Montalcino that year gave its prize to a "select red wine" called Brunello ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunello_di_Montalcino)).

**Curious details**
- **Three generations.** Giovanni Neri founded the estate in 1971; today his son Giacomo and grandsons Giovanni and Gianlorenzo run it, and a Brunello now carries his name, Giovanni Neri ([Fine+Rare](https://frw.co.uk/producer/612ec28006000000000005d6/casanova-di-neri)).
- **Optical sorting.** Every berry passes an optical sorter so only perfectly ripe fruit reaches the tank ([Fine+Rare](https://frw.co.uk/producer/612ec28006000000000005d6/casanova-di-neri)).
